Nizozemska navigacija: The TomTom Story from Palmtop to Global Mapping Giant

Le magazine slovène Monitor retrace l'histoire complète de TomTom, depuis ses origines comme Palmtop Software dans les années 1990 jusqu'à sa transformation en fournisseur mondial de données de localisation, en passant par l'icône TomTom GO qui a créé la catégorie des navigateurs portables et la transition difficile vers l'ère des smartphones.

Key takeaways
  • TomTom a été fondé à Amsterdam par quatre amis : Harold Goddijn, Corinne Vigreux, Peter-Frans Pauwels et Pieter Geelen, initialement sous le nom de Palmtop Software
  • À l'origine, l'entreprise développait des applications pour assistants personnels (Psion, Palm, Windows CE) : dictionnaires, outils financiers, listes de tâches
  • Le virage vers la navigation s'est fait avec l'arrivée des premiers récepteurs GPS commerciaux et des dlančniki (PDA) plus puissants
  • En 2002, TomTom lance son premier produit de navigation : TomTom Navigator, un package logiciel pour PDA avec récepteur GPS externe
  • En 2004, le TomTom GO révolutionne le marché : un navigateur autonome tout-en-un (écran tactile, GPS intégré, batterie) qui devient un des produits d'électronique grand public les plus vendus de l'histoire
  • Avec l'arrivée des smartphones, TomTom pivote vers la fourniture de données de localisation et de plateformes pour la conduite autonome
  • TomTom Traffic exploite les données anonymisées de millions d'appareils connectés, flottes automobiles et applications mobiles
  • Uber utilise les cartes TomTom ; la technologie TomTom est présente dans des centaines de millions de véhicules, smartphones et applications professionnelles dans le monde
2026-09-28 Monitor (Slovenia) Source article

Le «Google Maps» antique qui montre que tous les chemins ne menaient pas à Rome

Une équipe scientifique publie dans Nature Communications une analyse approfondie de la structure du réseau routier de l'Empire romain à son apogée, fruit d'un travail colossal croisant sources écrites — dont la table de Peutinger — et données archéologiques, révélant une organisation plus complexe qu'attendu entre planification impériale et héritages locaux.

Key takeaways
  • Le réseau routier de l'Empire romain comptait plus de 300 000 km à son apogée, quadrillant l'ensemble du bassin méditerranéen
  • En novembre 2025, la même équipe avait publié dans Scientific Data (Nature) un outil de navigation sur les routes romaines, surnommé « Google Maps antique », capable de calculer les temps de trajet entre villes antiques
  • Le nouvel article dans Nature Communications analyse en profondeur la structure de ce vaste réseau, croisant la table de Peutinger et des données de fouilles archéologiques
  • L'étude révèle que le réseau routier n'était pas uniformément planifié depuis Rome mais résultait d'un mélange entre planification impériale et héritages locaux
  • L'article est paru le 28 septembre 2026 dans la revue Nature Communications
2026-09-28 Vincent Bordenave (Le Figaro) Source article

Why Place Matters in Digital Health Communication

Geographic information systems help health organizations see and explain spatial patterns in public health, but maps and data alone do not reach people — effective digital health communication requires combining GIS analysis with place-based content strategies and production workflows.

Key takeaways
  • GIS helps health organizations identify and visualize spatial patterns in disease prevalence, access to care, and health outcomes
  • Maps and data alone are insufficient — they must be translated into accessible digital health content for target audiences
  • Effective digital health communication requires understanding the "place" dimension: where audiences live, work, and seek care
  • Production workflows for health content may involve analysts, writers, designers, developers, and video editors
  • Smaller teams may need to bring in outside specialists for tasks such as cleaning datasets or designing accessible maps
  • The integration of GIS with health communication supports targeted interventions and place-based public health messaging
2026-09-26 GISuser Source article

New map projections don't make the Mercator wrong

A letter to The Guardian defends the Mercator projection against charges of inherent bias, arguing it was fit for its original purpose and that its misuse reflects user laziness rather than cartographic prejudice.

Key takeaways
  • The transverse Mercator projection was created for European sailors and served that purpose effectively — its continued universal use is the fault of later users, not its creators
  • The Equal Earth projection is better suited to modern global representations, but that does not invalidate the Mercator for the tasks it was designed to accomplish
  • The claim of a "London-centric worldview" in maps is overstated: the international coordinate system centres on a point off west Africa, and UTM uses 60 different zone centres
  • Even the UK Ordnance Survey is not centred on London — its effective centre is in Lancashire
  • Map projections are tools, not political statements; choosing the right one depends on the use case, not on ideological correctness
2026-09-25 Paul Harwood (The Guardian) Source article

What Earthquake Response Needs From Geospatial Technology

Five critical gaps stand between geospatial technology and faster earthquake response: automated damage detection, unified data environments, offline-first field tools, dynamic population mapping, and pre-event readiness—addressable with today's technology but requiring better integration, standards, and funding.

Key takeaways
  • AI-assisted change detection can flag damaged buildings in minutes, but operates as post-request services rather than always-on pipelines
  • The most persistent geospatial failure is fragmentation: building footprints, population data, and road networks in separate, incompatible databases
  • Edge-first GIS applications are needed that cache base layers by default and support real-time field collection with sync-on-reconnect
  • Dynamic population mapping should combine census data, cell-phone mobility, and building-occupancy estimates rather than relying on static data
  • FEMA's GeoPlatform and OGC disaster pilots show that pre-built data environments work, but lack sustained investment
  • The geospatial industry must shift from delivering products after events to maintaining infrastructure before them
2026-09-24 Abigail Hart (Geo Week News) Source article

What Airborne Lidar Actually Sees in Ice

Geo Week News explains the surprising complexity of using airborne lidar to map ice: because ice is partly transparent to laser light, a single pulse can produce multiple echoes from different depths, creating both a measurement challenge and an unexpected tool for tracing internal ice layers.

Key takeaways
  • Ice is partly see-through to laser light — a single laser pulse can produce multiple echoes from the surface, internal layers, and the bottom of the ice
  • This transparency creates a measurement problem: scientists must determine which echo represents the true surface, as subsurface penetration can make the surface appear lower than it really is
  • Even a few inches of error per year matters enormously when measuring ice thinning in Greenland and Antarctica, where the difference between "stable" and "melting fast" is only a few inches per year
  • The same property that makes lidar tricky on ice also makes it powerful: it can detect internal layers within the ice, including volcanic ash markers, connecting drill sites across large stretches
  • Different ice types pose different challenges: snow scatters light, meltwater ponds act like mirrors, and sea ice shifts and piles into ridges
  • Radar complements lidar by reaching the bottom of ice sheets a mile or more thick, while lidar needs clear air — clouds, fog, and blowing snow can make a flight useless
2026-09-22 Geo Week News Source article
